abstract: Software is one of the most powerful tools that we humans have at our disposal; it allows a skilled programmer to interact with the world in complex and profound ways. At the same time, thanks to improvements in large language models (LLMs), there has also been a rapid development in AI agents that interact with and affect change in their surrounding environments. In this paper, we introduce OpenHands (f.k.a. OpenDevin), a platform for the development of powerful and flexible AI agents that interact with the world in similar ways to those of a human developer: by writing code, interacting with a command line, and browsing the web. We describe how the platform allows for the implementation of new agents, safe interaction with sandboxed environments for code execution, coordination between multiple agents, and incorporation of evaluation benchmarks. Based on our currently incorporated benchmarks, we perform an evaluation of agents over 15 challenging tasks, including software engineering (e.g., Swe-bench) and web browsing (e.g., WebArena), among others. Released under the permissive MIT license, OpenHands is a community project spanning academia and industry with more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors.

sections.body: The introduction states that OpenHands is a community platform for building generalist and specialist AI agents that interact with the world through software. It lists five features: an event-stream interaction mechanism (§2.1), a Docker-sandboxed runtime with bash, a web browser, and an IPython server (§2.2), an agent interface for editing code, running code, and browsing (§2.3), multi-agent delegation (§2.4), and an evaluation framework (§4). It reports 32K GitHub stars, more than 2.1K contributions, and over 188 contributors, and says the project is released under the MIT license.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: OpenHands is a community platform for building agents that write code, use a shell, and browse the web.

sections.body: An agent maps the current state, which holds a chronological event stream of actions and observations, to a next action through its step function. Core actions are IPythonRunCellAction and CmdRunAction for Python and bash, plus BrowserInteractiveAction for browsing, following CodeAct and BrowserGym. Each task session runs in a securely isolated Docker container, where a REST API server executes actions and returns observations. The section also describes an AgentSkills library of utilities such as `edit_file`, `scroll_up`, `scroll_down`, `parse_image`, and `parse_pdf`, and the AgentDelegateAction type for delegating subtasks to another agent.
sections.heading: OpenHands Architecture
sections.headline: Agents are defined by a step function over an event stream, and actions run in a Docker sandbox that returns observations.

sections.body: CodeActAgent is the default generalist agent. It can converse with humans or act by executing bash, Python, or browser code. The Browsing Agent is described as similar to the WebArena agent, with improved observations and actions, using only zero-shot prompting. The GPTSwarm agent is included, with nodes as operations and edges as collaboration pathways. Micro agents reuse an existing generalist agent and add specialized prompts. The section gives no quantitative results for these agents.
sections.heading: AgentHub: A Hub of Community-Contributed Agents
sections.headline: The AgentHub ships a default CodeAct agent, a browsing agent, a graph-based agent, and a template for micro agents.

sections.body: The evaluation integrates 15 benchmarks covering software engineering, web browsing, and miscellaneous assistance, and compares against open-source baselines without benchmark-specific prompt engineering. On SWE-bench Lite, CodeActAgent v1.8 using claude-3.5-sonnet resolves 26% of issues, with hint text excluded. On HumanEvalFix Python, it fixes 79.3% of bugs in 0-shot evaluation, while SWE-Agent reports 87.7% with a 1-shot demonstration. The paper states that the browsing agent is competitive on WebArena among LLM agents using domain-general prompting, and the same agent is used across task categories without modifying its system prompt. Limitations include that OpenHands 'may not achieve top performance in every category'.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Across 15 benchmarks, the CodeActAgent resolves 26% of software engineering issues and fixes 79.3% of Python bugs.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the platform's components: a powerful interaction mechanism, a sandboxed environment, agent skills, multi-agent collaboration, and an evaluation framework. It claims these accelerate research and real-world use of agentic AI systems. The conclusion notes that safe and reliable agent development remains a challenge and points to the limitations discussed in the appendix. It does not introduce new results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: OpenHands is presented as a community platform that accelerates research and applications of agentic AI systems.

sections.body: Appendix A lists future work: multi-modality, stronger agents, improved file editing on long files, browsing improvements such as reward models and Reflexion, and automatic workflow generation. Appendix B gives an ethics statement emphasizing evaluation and human oversight. Appendix C covers related agent frameworks. Appendix D describes the graphical user interface, and Appendix E describes integration tests that mock LLM calls by exact prompt match. Appendix F details the Docker runtime client-server workflow and image tagging. Appendices G through K give full GPQA results, the CodeActSWEAgent demonstration, the AgentSkills list, BrowserGym actions, and browsing agent prompts.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers limitations, ethics, related work, the graphical interface, integration tests, runtime image building, graduate-level benchmark results, prompts, skills, and BrowserGym actions.
